Apple___Apple_scab.description: A common fungal disease of apple leaves and fruit that is worst in cool, wet springs. It rarely kills trees but can defoliate them and ruin fruit quality.
symptoms: Olive-green to brown velvety spots on the leaves, often along the veins
Spots turn dark and the leaf may curl, yellow and drop early
Dark, corky, sometimes cracked scabs on fruit
Apple___Apple_scab.causes: The fungus Venturia inaequalis, which overwinters in fallen leaves and spreads by spores during spring rain.
treatment_organic: Rake up and destroy or compost fallen leaves in autumn to remove the overwintering fungus
Prune to open the canopy so leaves dry quickly after rain
Sulfur- or copper-based products approved for organic use can protect new growth when applied before infection periods
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for apple scab, applied from bud break through early summer during wet weather
Always follow the product label and your local extension service's spray calendar
prevention: Plant scab-resistant apple varieties
Remove fallen leaves and avoid overhead irrigation
Space and prune trees for good air flow

Apple___Black_rot.description: A fungal disease that causes leaf spots (frogeye leaf spot), fruit rot and limb cankers. It builds up on dead wood and mummified fruit left in the orchard.
symptoms: Small purple spots on leaves that enlarge into tan-brown centres with a purple border ("frogeye")
Firm brown rot on fruit, often starting at the blossom end, with dark rings
Sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches
Apple___Black_rot.causes: The fungus Botryosphaeria obtusa, which survives in cankers, dead wood and shrivelled fruit and spreads in warm, wet weather.
treatment_organic: Prune out dead or cankered wood and remove mummified fruit from the tree and ground
Destroy prunings rather than leaving them near the orchard
Copper- or sulfur-based products approved for organic use may help protect leaves
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for black rot / frogeye leaf spot, timed as advised by local extension guidance
Follow the product label exactly
prevention: Keep trees vigorous with proper watering and fertilisation
Remove dead wood, fire-blight strikes and fruit mummies every winter
Avoid wounding trees, which gives the fungus an entry point

Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.description: A rust disease that needs two hosts: apple and juniper (eastern red cedar). Spores blow from galls on junipers to apple leaves in spring.
symptoms: Bright yellow-orange spots on the upper leaf surface in late spring
Spots enlarge and develop small tube-like structures on the leaf underside
Heavy infection causes early leaf drop and weaker trees
Apple___Cedar_apple_rust.causes: The fungus Gymnosporangium juniperi-virginianae, which alternates between juniper galls and apple leaves.
treatment_organic: Remove visible rust galls from nearby junipers in late winter
Pick off badly infected leaves on young trees
Sulfur-based products approved for organic use can give some protection
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for rust on apple, applied from pink bud to early summer
Follow label directions and local extension advice
prevention: Plant rust-resistant apple varieties
Where practical, avoid planting apples close to juniper or red cedar
Monitor junipers for orange gelatinous galls after spring rain

Apple___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this apple leaf.
prevention: Keep monitoring leaves weekly, especially after rainy periods
Clean up fallen leaves and fruit to reduce overwintering diseases
Prune for good airflow and sunlight penetration

Blueberry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this blueberry leaf.
prevention: Keep soil acidic and well drained, and mulch to retain moisture
Prune out old, weak or dead canes each winter
Inspect leaves and fruit regularly for spots or rot

Cherry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this cherry leaf.
prevention: Prune to keep the canopy open and dry
Water at the base of the tree rather than over the leaves
Check leaves for white powdery growth during warm, humid weather

Cherry___Powdery_mildew.description: A fungal disease that grows on the surface of young leaves and fruit. It favours warm days, humid nights and dense canopies.
symptoms: White, powdery patches on leaves, usually starting on the underside
Leaves may curl, pucker or become brittle
Powdery or russeted patches on fruit near harvest
Cherry___Powdery_mildew.causes: The fungus Podosphaera clandestina (Podosphaera cerasi), which overwinters on the tree and spreads by wind-blown spores.
treatment_organic: Prune out heavily infected shoots and improve airflow
Sulfur-based products, horticultural oils or potassium bicarbonate approved for organic use can suppress mildew
Avoid excess nitrogen, which promotes soft, susceptible growth
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for cherry powdery mildew, rotating modes of action to slow resistance
Follow the product label and local extension spray timing
prevention: Manage irrigation so the canopy does not stay humid
Remove root suckers and water sprouts, which are often infected first
Begin monitoring from shoot growth in spring

Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.description: One of the most yield-limiting foliar diseases of maize in warm, humid regions. It survives on corn residue left on the soil surface.
symptoms: Small tan spots that grow into long, narrow, rectangular grey-to-tan lesions
Lesions are limited by the leaf veins, giving straight edges
Lesions merge and blight whole leaves in severe cases
Corn___Cercospora_leaf_spot Gray_leaf_sp.causes: The fungus Cercospora zeae-maydis, favoured by long periods of high humidity, warm temperatures and corn-on-corn planting.
treatment_organic: Rotate to a non-host crop for at least one year
Bury or break down infected residue where soil conservation allows
treatment_chemical: Foliar fungicides labelled for gray leaf spot, when disease reaches the upper leaves around tasselling in susceptible hybrids
Follow label directions and local extension thresholds
prevention: Plant resistant or tolerant hybrids
Rotate crops and manage residue
Scout fields regularly from mid-season

Corn___Common_rust.description: A widespread rust disease of maize. Spores are carried long distances by wind, and it is favoured by cool, humid weather.
symptoms: Small, oval, cinnamon-brown powdery pustules on both leaf surfaces
Pustules turn dark brown to black as the plant matures
Heavily infected leaves may yellow and die early
Corn___Common_rust.causes: The fungus Puccinia sorghi, spread by windborne spores during cool (16-23 C) weather with heavy dew.
treatment_organic: Usually no action is needed on tolerant hybrids
Maintain balanced nutrition to keep plants vigorous
treatment_chemical: Foliar fungicides labelled for common rust may be justified on susceptible sweet corn or seed corn early in the season
Follow label directions and local extension guidance
prevention: Plant rust-resistant hybrids
Plant early so the crop matures before rust builds up
Scout leaves regularly in cool, humid periods

Corn___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this maize leaf.
prevention: Rotate maize with other crops to break disease cycles
Choose hybrids with resistance to common local diseases
Scout fields regularly, especially in humid weather

Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.description: A fungal leaf disease of maize that can cause significant yield loss if it reaches the upper leaves before grain fill.
symptoms: Long, cigar-shaped, grey-green to tan lesions, 2.5-15 cm long
Lesions start on lower leaves and move upward
Dark spore masses on lesions in humid weather
Corn___Northern_Leaf_Blight.causes: The fungus Exserohilum turcicum, which survives on infected residue and spreads in moderate temperatures with long dew periods.
treatment_organic: Rotate crops and manage infected residue
Remove volunteer maize plants
treatment_chemical: Foliar fungicides labelled for northern leaf blight, if lesions appear on upper leaves around tasselling
Follow label directions and local extension thresholds
prevention: Plant hybrids with resistance to northern leaf blight
Rotate away from maize for at least one season
Scout from knee height onward

Grape___Black_rot.description: A destructive fungal disease of grapes in warm, humid climates. It can destroy most of the crop if not managed early in the season.
symptoms: Small reddish-brown circular spots on leaves with a darker border and tiny black dots
Berries turn brown, then shrivel into hard black 'mummies'
Elongated dark lesions on shoots and leaf stems
Grape___Black_rot.causes: The fungus Guignardia bidwellii (Phyllosticta ampelicida), which overwinters in mummified berries and spreads in rain.
treatment_organic: Remove all mummified berries from vines and the ground during dormant pruning
Remove infected leaves and clusters as soon as they appear
Copper- or sulfur-based products approved for organic use can protect new growth
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for grape black rot from early shoot growth until berries are well formed
Follow the product label and local extension spray programme
prevention: Remove mummies and infected canes every winter
Train and prune vines for good air circulation and sun exposure
Control weeds under the trellis to speed drying

Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).description: A grapevine trunk disease caused by wood-infecting fungi. It weakens vines over years and can kill them suddenly in hot weather.
symptoms: 'Tiger-stripe' leaves: yellow or red bands between the veins that later dry out
Small dark spots ('measles') on berries, which may crack and dry
Dark streaking in the wood when trunks or cordons are cut
Grape___Esca_(Black_Measles).causes: Several wood-decay fungi (including Phaeomoniella chlamydospora and Phaeoacremonium species) that enter through pruning wounds.
treatment_organic: Cut out and destroy dead or infected wood well below visible symptoms
Retrain new trunks from healthy suckers where vines are badly affected
Protect large pruning wounds with a wound sealant or approved biological protectant
treatment_chemical: There is no curative chemical treatment for infected vines
Registered pruning-wound protectants can reduce new infections; follow label and extension advice
prevention: Prune in dry weather and late in the dormant season when wounds heal faster
Avoid large pruning cuts and remove prunings from the vineyard
Plant clean, certified nursery stock

Grape___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this grape leaf.
prevention: Prune and train vines for an open, airy canopy
Remove mummified berries and dead wood each winter
Monitor leaves closely during warm, wet weather

Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.description: A fungal leaf spot of grapes, most common in warm, humid regions and late in the season. Severe cases cause early leaf drop and weaker vines.
symptoms: Irregular dark red-brown to black spots on leaves
Spots merge into larger dead (necrotic) patches, often with a yellow edge
Dark fungal growth on the leaf underside; early leaf fall
Grape___Leaf_blight_(Isariopsis_Leaf_Spo.causes: The fungus Pseudocercospora vitis (formerly Isariopsis clavispora), which survives on fallen leaves and spreads in humid weather.
treatment_organic: Collect and destroy fallen infected leaves
Improve canopy airflow by shoot thinning and leaf removal
Copper-based products approved for organic use can protect leaves
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for grape leaf spots, as advised by local extension services
Follow the product label
prevention: Remove leaf litter after harvest
Avoid overhead irrigation
Maintain balanced nutrition and vine vigour

Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).description: The most serious disease of citrus worldwide. It is spread by the Asian citrus psyllid, has no cure, and infected trees decline and eventually die.
symptoms: Blotchy, asymmetric yellow mottling on leaves (unlike the symmetric pattern of nutrient deficiency)
Yellow shoots, small upright leaves and twig dieback
Small, lopsided, bitter fruit that stays partly green
Orange___Haunglongbing_(Citrus_greening).causes: The bacterium Candidatus Liberibacter asiaticus, spread by the Asian citrus psyllid and by grafting infected plant material.
treatment_organic: There is no cure; infected trees should be removed to protect nearby trees
Report suspected cases to your local agricultural or plant-health authority (it is a regulated disease in many countries)
treatment_chemical: No chemical cures the disease
Area-wide control of the psyllid vector with registered insecticides, coordinated by local authorities and extension services
prevention: Buy only certified disease-free citrus nursery trees
Inspect new growth regularly for psyllids
Do not move citrus plants or plant material between regions

Peach___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of peach and other stone fruits, worst on sandy soils in warm, wet and windy weather.
symptoms: Small, angular, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn purple-brown
Spot centres fall out, giving a 'shot-hole' appearance; leaves yellow and drop
Pitted, cracked spots on fruit
Peach___Bacterial_spot.causes: The bacterium Xanthomonas arboricola pv. pruni, which overwinters in twig cankers and spreads by wind-driven rain.
treatment_organic: Prune out cankered twigs during dry weather
Copper-based products approved for organic use, applied at the timings recommended by extension services, can reduce spread (copper can injure peach leaves, so follow guidance closely)
treatment_chemical: Bactericides labelled for bacterial spot on stone fruit, following local extension spray programmes
Follow the product label to avoid leaf injury
prevention: Plant resistant or less susceptible varieties
Keep trees vigorous with adequate (not excessive) nitrogen
Use windbreaks to reduce wind-blown rain injury

Peach___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this peach leaf.
prevention: Prune for an open-centre canopy with good airflow
Remove cankered twigs and mummified fruit during winter
Inspect leaves after spells of wet, windy weather

Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of pepper and tomato that thrives in warm, wet weather and spreads quickly by splashing water and handling wet plants.
symptoms: Small, water-soaked spots on leaves that turn brown with a yellow halo
Infected leaves yellow and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald
Raised, scabby spots on fruit
Pepper,_bell___Bacterial_spot.causes: Xanthomonas bacteria, carried on seed and transplants and spread by rain splash, overhead irrigation and handling.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy badly infected plants and leaves
Avoid working among plants when they are wet
Copper-based products approved for organic use can slow spread when applied early
treatment_chemical: Bactericides labelled for bacterial spot on pepper, as recommended by local extension services
Follow the product label; resistance to copper exists in some regions
prevention: Use certified disease-free seed and transplants, and resistant varieties
Use drip irrigation instead of overhead watering
Rotate away from pepper and tomato for 2-3 years

Pepper,_bell___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this bell pepper leaf.
prevention: Water at the base of the plant and avoid wetting leaves
Rotate peppers with non-related crops
Check leaves regularly for spots, especially in warm, wet weather

Potato___Early_blight.description: A common fungal disease of potato and tomato that usually starts on older, lower leaves, especially on stressed plants.
symptoms: Dark brown spots with concentric rings (a 'target' pattern) on older leaves
Yellowing around the spots; affected leaves die and drop
Dark, sunken, dry lesions on tubers
Potato___Early_blight.causes: The fungus Alternaria solani, which survives in soil and crop residue and spreads in alternating wet and dry weather.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected lower leaves
Keep plants well nourished and watered to reduce stress
Copper-based products approved for organic use can slow spread
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for early blight, started when the first spots appear
Follow the product label and local extension advice
prevention: Rotate potatoes with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years
Use certified seed tubers and destroy crop debris after harvest
Avoid overhead irrigation late in the day

Potato___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this potato leaf.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers
Rotate potatoes with non-related crops
Scout leaves often during cool, wet weather when late blight can spread quickly

Potato___Late_blight.description: The disease behind the Irish Potato Famine. In cool, wet weather it can destroy a potato or tomato crop within days, so act quickly.
symptoms: Large, dark, water-soaked patches on leaves that spread fast
White fuzzy growth on the leaf underside in humid conditions
Firm reddish-brown rot on tubers
Potato___Late_blight.causes: The water mould Phytophthora infestans, spread by airborne spores from infected plants, cull piles and infected seed tubers.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy (do not compost) infected plants immediately
Copper-based products approved for organic use can protect healthy foliage
Alert neighbouring growers, as spores travel long distances
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for late blight, applied preventively when local disease forecasts warn of risk
Contact your local agricultural officer promptly for region-specific advice
prevention: Plant certified seed tubers and resistant varieties
Destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles
Hill soil over tubers and harvest only after vines are completely dead

Raspberry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this raspberry leaf.
prevention: Remove old fruiting canes after harvest
Keep rows narrow for good airflow
Plant certified disease-free canes in well-drained soil

Soybean___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this soybean leaf.
prevention: Rotate soybean with cereals such as maize
Choose varieties resistant to common local diseases
Scout fields regularly through the season

Squash___Powdery_mildew.description: A very common fungal disease of squash, pumpkin, melon and cucumber. It reduces yield and fruit quality by killing leaves early.
symptoms: White, talc-like powdery spots on leaves and stems
Spots spread to cover whole leaves, which yellow and dry out
Fruit may be small, poorly flavoured or sunburnt
Squash___Powdery_mildew.causes: Fungi such as Podosphaera xanthii, whose wind-borne spores thrive in dense plantings, shade and high humidity (no free water needed).
treatment_organic: Remove badly infected leaves
Sulfur, horticultural oils, potassium bicarbonate or biological fungicides approved for organic use can suppress mildew
Do not apply oils and sulfur close together or in hot weather, as leaves may burn
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for cucurbit powdery mildew, rotating modes of action to avoid resistance
Follow the product label
prevention: Plant resistant varieties
Space plants for airflow and full sun
Avoid excess nitrogen fertiliser

Strawberry___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this strawberry leaf.
prevention: Plant certified disease-free plants in well-drained beds
Remove old, dead leaves after harvest
Use drip irrigation and mulch to keep leaves and fruit dry

Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.description: A fungal leaf disease of strawberry. Heavy infection weakens plants, reducing vigour and next season's yield.
symptoms: Many small, irregular purple spots on the upper leaf surface
Spots merge and the leaf looks burnt or 'scorched' between them
Leaves dry and curl upward; lesions can also appear on stems and fruit caps
Strawberry___Leaf_scorch.causes: The fungus Diplocarpon earlianum, which survives on infected leaves and spreads by splashing water.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected leaves, and renovate beds after harvest
Avoid overhead watering
Copper-based products approved for organic use may give some protection
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for strawberry leaf scorch, applied as advised by local extension services
Follow the product label
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and certified plants
Space plants for airflow and control weeds
Rotate strawberry plantings every few years

Tomato___Bacterial_spot.description: A bacterial disease of tomato and pepper that is hard to control once established in warm, rainy weather.
symptoms: Small, dark, greasy-looking spots on leaves, sometimes with a yellow halo
Spots merge and leaves turn yellow, then brown
Raised, scabby brown spots on green fruit
Tomato___Bacterial_spot.causes: Xanthomonas bacteria, introduced on seed or transplants and spread by rain splash, overhead irrigation and handling wet plants.
treatment_organic: Remove infected leaves and badly affected plants
Avoid handling plants when wet
Copper-based products approved for organic use can slow spread when applied early
treatment_chemical: Bactericides labelled for bacterial spot on tomato, following local extension recommendations
Follow the product label; copper-resistant strains occur in some regions
prevention: Use disease-free seed and transplants
Use drip irrigation and stake plants to keep leaves dry
Rotate away from tomato and pepper for 2-3 years

Tomato___Early_blight.description: One of the most common tomato diseases. It starts on lower leaves and moves upward, weakening plants and exposing fruit to sunscald.
symptoms: Brown spots with concentric 'target' rings on older leaves
Yellow tissue around the spots; lower leaves drop
Dark, sunken lesions on stems and at the stem end of fruit
Tomato___Early_blight.causes: The fungus Alternaria (A. solani / A. linariae), which survives on crop debris and in soil.
treatment_organic: Remove infected lower leaves and mulch the soil to stop spores splashing up
Keep plants well fed and watered to reduce stress
Copper-based products approved for organic use can slow spread
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for early blight on tomato, started when first symptoms appear
Follow the product label and local extension advice
prevention: Rotate with non-solanaceous crops for 2-3 years
Stake or cage plants and prune lower leaves for airflow
Remove and destroy plant debris at season end

Tomato___healthy.description: No signs of disease were detected on this tomato leaf.
prevention: Water at the base of plants and mulch the soil
Stake plants and prune for airflow
Rotate tomatoes with non-related crops each year

Tomato___Late_blight.description: A fast-spreading, destructive disease of tomato and potato. In cool, wet weather it can kill plants within days.
symptoms: Large, irregular, greasy grey-green patches on leaves that quickly turn brown
White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides in humid weather
Firm, greasy brown blotches on fruit
Tomato___Late_blight.causes: The water mould Phytophthora infestans, carried long distances on wind from infected tomato or potato plants.
treatment_organic: Remove and bag or destroy infected plants immediately (do not compost)
Copper-based products approved for organic use can protect healthy plants
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for late blight, applied preventively when disease is reported nearby
Contact your local agricultural officer promptly for region-specific advice
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and healthy transplants
Do not grow tomatoes near potatoes, and destroy volunteer potatoes
Keep leaves dry with drip irrigation and good spacing

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.description: A fungal disease most common in greenhouses and high tunnels, where humidity stays high.
symptoms: Pale green to yellow patches on the upper leaf surface
Olive-green to grey-brown velvety mould on the matching leaf underside
Leaves wither and drop; fruit is rarely affected
Tomato___Leaf_Mold.causes: The fungus Passalora fulva (Cladosporium fulvum), favoured by relative humidity above 85%.
treatment_organic: Remove and destroy infected leaves
Increase ventilation and reduce humidity in greenhouses
Copper-based products approved for organic use can protect remaining leaves
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for leaf mold on tomato, as recommended by local extension services
Follow the product label
prevention: Keep greenhouse humidity below 85% and ventilate well
Space and prune plants for airflow
Plant resistant varieties and clean the greenhouse between crops

Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.description: A very common fungal disease that strips tomato plants of their leaves from the bottom up during wet, warm weather.
symptoms: Many small circular spots with dark borders and grey-white centres on lower leaves
Tiny black dots (fungal fruiting bodies) in the spot centres
Leaves yellow, wither and drop, exposing fruit to sunscald
Tomato___Septoria_leaf_spot.causes: The fungus Septoria lycopersici, which survives on plant debris and spreads by splashing water.
treatment_organic: Remove infected lower leaves promptly
Mulch around plants to reduce soil splash
Copper-based products approved for organic use can slow spread
treatment_chemical: Protective fungicides labelled for Septoria leaf spot on tomato
Follow the product label and local extension advice
prevention: Rotate away from tomatoes for at least one year
Remove and destroy plant debris after harvest
Water at soil level and avoid working among wet plants

Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.description: Not a disease but a pest: tiny mites that suck sap from leaves. Populations explode in hot, dry, dusty conditions.
symptoms: Fine yellow or white speckling (stippling) on leaves
Leaves turn bronze or yellow and dry out
Fine webbing on leaf undersides and between leaves in heavy infestations
Tomato___Spider_mites Two-spotted_spider.causes: The two-spotted spider mite (Tetranychus urticae), favoured by heat, drought stress and dust, and by sprays that kill its natural predators.
treatment_organic: Spray leaf undersides with a strong jet of water to knock mites off
Insecticidal soaps or horticultural oils approved for organic use, covering leaf undersides
Encourage or release natural predators such as predatory mites
treatment_chemical: Miticides labelled for spider mites on tomato, only when monitoring shows they are needed
Avoid broad-spectrum insecticides that kill natural enemies; follow the product label
prevention: Keep plants well watered to avoid drought stress
Reduce dust on and around plants
Check leaf undersides regularly in hot, dry weather

Tomato___Target_Spot.description: A fungal disease of tomato in warm, humid regions. It affects leaves, stems and fruit and can cause heavy leaf loss.
symptoms: Small brown spots on leaves that grow into lesions with light-brown centres and concentric rings
Lesions often have a yellow halo; leaves may drop
Sunken, pitted spots on fruit
Tomato___Target_Spot.causes: The fungus Corynespora cassiicola, which survives on crop debris and other host plants and spreads in humid weather.
treatment_organic: Remove infected lower leaves and crop debris
Improve airflow by pruning and staking
Copper-based products approved for organic use may slow spread
treatment_chemical: Fungicides labelled for target spot on tomato, as recommended by local extension services
Follow the product label and rotate modes of action
prevention: Rotate crops and destroy plant debris after harvest
Avoid overhead irrigation and excessive nitrogen
Control weeds that may host the fungus

Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.description: A very stable, highly contagious virus. It spreads easily on hands, tools and clothing, and there is no cure for infected plants.
symptoms: Light and dark green mottled or mosaic pattern on leaves
Leaves may be curled, distorted or fern-like
Stunted plants, reduced yield and unevenly ripening fruit
Tomato___Tomato_mosaic_virus.causes: Tomato mosaic virus (ToMV), spread mechanically through contact, contaminated tools and infected seed, and able to survive in plant debris.
treatment_organic: There is no cure: remove and destroy infected plants
Wash hands and disinfect tools after handling suspect plants
treatment_chemical: No chemical treatment cures viral infections
Focus on sanitation and resistant varieties
prevention: Plant resistant varieties and certified virus-free seed
Disinfect tools, stakes and hands regularly
Avoid using tobacco products near plants

Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.description: A devastating whitefly-transmitted virus of tomato in warm regions. Plants infected early may produce almost no fruit.
symptoms: Upward curling and cupping of leaves
Yellow leaf edges and small, crumpled leaves
Stunted, bushy plants with flower drop and poor fruit set
Tomato___Tomato_Yellow_Leaf_Curl_Virus.causes: Tomato yellow leaf curl virus (TYLCV), spread by the silverleaf whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
treatment_organic: There is no cure: remove and destroy infected plants promptly to reduce spread
Use insect-proof netting, reflective mulches and yellow sticky traps against whiteflies
treatment_chemical: No chemical cures the virus
Whitefly control with registered insecticides as part of an integrated plan guided by local extension services
prevention: Plant TYLCV-resistant varieties and whitefly-free transplants
Remove weeds and crop residues that host whiteflies
Leave a host-free period between tomato crops where possible
